news.title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything
news.text:
Marine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersEurope’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everythingNathalie TocciIf far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.

Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.

In addition to Spain, France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.

Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able to form a majority in the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.

This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party was punished at the polls and the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, after Viktor Orbán was ousted in a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats, scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’s recent victory in eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times.

But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirm Giorgia Meloni as Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.

If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology.

View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Friedrich Merz in Berlin after Burnham ‘opened the door to Britain rejoining the EU’ Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAAnd it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outside Italy is that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.

The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade, publicly recognise that Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done.

It has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone.

Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist

news.title: Trump stated strong personal animosity between Zelenskyy and Putin
news.text:
US President Donald Trump stated a "strong animosity" between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said this during a speech to Republican Party supporters in Ohio ahead of the November US congressional elections, writes RBC.

“There is a very strong mutual animosity between the two leaders,” he said.

Despite this, the head of the White House stated that a peace agreement “will be concluded.”

Before flying to Ohio, Trump said that Moscow and Kyiv want to conclude an agreement, but "don't know how."

“But we will make sure that they conclude a deal,” he added.

At the same time, the US President stated that Putin "wants to conclude a deal more than Zelenskyy."

Additionally, answering questions from journalists, the American leader urged Zelenskyy to focus on concluding a deal, rather than talking about it.

“And here's what I think. Zelenskyy should focus on concluding a deal, not talking about it,” he said.

This is not the first time the US president has stated animosity between the Russian and Ukrainian leaders. He expressed a similar opinion in March during a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the White House.

news.title: Eric Trump trashes ABC over ‘bulls–t hit piece,’ backs call for FCC probe into revised story on family biz
news.text:
Eric Trump expressed support for a federal probe into a botched story from ABC News about his family’s business dealings with defense contractor Anduril Industries.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to investigate what led to an erroneous report published on the Disney-owned network’s website last week with the headline “Trump sons’ investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election.” 

The report was initially deleted without explanation and then republished with a correction.

“Thank you @berniemoreno — can’t wait to participate!” Eric Trump reacted Monday on X.

“You can’t publish a bulls–t hit-piece, let it spread and go viral, then delete it 24 hours later, under the cover of darkness with no explanation or apology. Who approved it? Has the author been fired? @ABC owes us answers,” he continued.

In a letter to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, Moreno demanded accountability for the network’s report and questioned whether ABC News violated its obligations as a broadcaster.

“Thus, I urge the Commission to open a formal investigation into ABC News’s political hit job. We must know who signed off on the publication of this false story, who may have asked to profit from the attack, and whether ABC News’s conduct violated its obligations as a licensee,” Moreno said.

The letter followed ABC News’ decision to remove a report examining investments tied to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. The original Wednesday article claimed companies connected to the president’s sons had secured billions in government contracts, including through venture capital firm 1789 Capital.

Moreno specifically challenged the original report’s characterization of Anduril’s financing, arguing that the network had misrepresented the company’s investment activity and unfairly associated the Trump family with federal contracting decisions.

The controversy centered on ABC News’ original claim that 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. serves as a partner, acquired a major strike in Anduril through a $2.5 billion investment. 

The figure instead represented Anduril’s broader fundraising round, while 1789 Capital’s investment was approximately $50 million.

ABC News republished a substantially revised article Friday, acknowledging errors involving investments, government contracts and the chronology of events. 

The updated version also clarified that Trump Jr. does not serve on the firm’s investment decision-making committee. 

The new headline reads, “New shipyard announced amid earlier Democratic concerns about potential conflicts of interest,” though the original reporter’s byline was replaced with “ABC News.”

A 1789 source told Fox News Digital that an ABC News journalist involved with the story defended it over the phone before the story itself was deleted. 

Semafor similarly reported Sunday that editors initially stood by the published story, according to emails between ABC News investigative reporter Nathan Lee, who authored the original story, and an Anduril spokesperson. 

That would contradict the network’s notion to other media reporters that the story was published “prematurely.”

ABC News did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

news.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms Debates Alone in Unusual Georgia Governor Showdown
news.text: Georgia Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms took the debate stage Monday without her Republican opponent, standing beside an empty podium as she answered questions on the eve of early voting in the Peach State. “Rick Jackson is the first gubernatorial candidate not to stand here in 32 years," Bottoms said in her opening remarks. “He would rather hide behind his billions than explain to you his record of making billions off the taxpayers of Georgia.” The debate lasted less than 30 minutes and featured two journalists questioning Bottoms, who appeared alone after GOP gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson declined to participate. Jackson's campaign said he had a scheduling conflict and was campaigning in the Savannah area, according to WSB-TV. The Republican spent Monday touring Georgia, visiting Atlanta, Macon, Columbus and Savannah before heading to Columbia County. When asked about his decision not to attend the debate, Jackson told reporters Monday, “Out of probably 10,000 people I've talked to, not one of them has mentioned anything about a debate because that's not important to the people.” Newsweek reached out to Jackson and Bottoms’ campaigns for comment Monday night. The candidates previously debated on October 6 during a town hall hosted by Atlanta News First, where they answered questions from undecided voters across Georgia on a range of issues. The town hall was described as likely their only debate. Monday's event was part of the Atlanta Press Club’s Loudermilk-Young Debate Series. Why the Georgia Governor's Race Matters The Peach State battle for the governor’s mansion is shaping up to be closely contested as candidates vie to succeed term-limited Republican Governor Brian Kemp. Jackson is founder of Jackson Healthcare, a medical staffing company, and has positioned himself as a political outsider. Bottoms served as Atlanta’s mayor from 2018 to 2022 and later as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden. Jackson currently leads Bottoms 49 percent to 47 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ’s polling average. A recent YouGov poll also found a tight race, with Jackson receiving 45 percent support and Bottoms 44 percent. Nine percent of respondents were undecided. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. The contest also carries historical significance. If Bottoms wins, she would become the first Black woman to serve as governor in the United States. Jackson has repeatedly criticized Bottoms' record as Atlanta mayor. “Keisha nearly destroyed Atlanta,” Jackson wrote on X Monday. “We aren’t going to let her destroy Georgia, but only with your vote.” President Donald Trump is scheduled to attend a midterm campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, on Friday to campaign for Jackson and Republican Senate nominee Mike Collins as Republicans seek to retain control of the governor’s office and defend their Senate majority. Early voting begins in Georgia on Tuesday, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Commander and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The Democratic nominee answered questions alone after her opponent skipped the debate on the eve of Georgia’s early voting.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Bill Maher, 70, Brags of New Turn in Relationship With Trump
news.text:
Bill Maher has bragged about a dramatic change in his complicated relationship with President Donald Trump.

Maher, 70, was invited to the White House in 2025 for a dinner brokered by their mutual friend Kid Rock. After the event, Maher said Trump, 80, was “gracious and measured,” and not like the “person who plays a crazy person on TV.”

Relations between the pair have not gone smoothly since. In a lengthy Truth Social rant in February, Trump called Maher a “lightweight” and “ANTI TRUMP,” The president also said it was “a total waste of time for me to have this jerk at the White House.”

Maher compared Trump to a “redneck” emperor over his UFC birthday bash in June and said the president has done “things that are racist, misogynistic, anti-democratic and corrupt.”

As recently as September, Trump put Maher on blast on Truth Social, calling out his ratings for Real Time. “Bill Maher’s ratings are so low that it is hard to believe his show can continue,” Trump posted. “In many ways it’s SAD because, in actuality, I like him. Republicans should stop using him as a sounding board, however. It makes them look sooo weak and foolish!”

However, during Monday’s episode of his Club Random podcast, Maher revealed another White House dinner is imminent.

Maher spoke with Hollywood power agent Ari Emanuel, also a friend of Trump, when talk turned to their individual relationships with the president.

“I’m having dinner with him again next week,” Maher bragged to Emanuel, who told the comedian that he, in turn, was having conversations with Trump over a “rebate I think needs to happen for California and for the country.... and he’s on board with it.”

Emanuel added of Trump, “He’s 80 years old, this guy, and I don’t know if you felt it, he’s a workaholic.”

Maher laughed and said, “Well, in his way. And a lot of that work is toward things we don’t approve of.” The comic added, “And we’ll tell him.”

The podcast host then remarked, “It’s so weird, after the first dinner, you know, I went back to doing what I do,” referencing his public commentary on Trump.

Emanuel said, “He probably screamed at you,” with Maher saying, “It never stops. He tried to stop me from getting the Mark Twain award.”

Ahead of the announcement that Maher would receive the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, Trump’s communications director Steven Cheung claimed it was “Literally FAKE NEWS.” Maher received the award in June, and Trump did not attend the event.

On the red carpet, Maher said he was not shocked by the Trump administration’s reaction to his award. 

“I wouldn’t be surprised if it happens again before the show starts,” Maher said at the time. “Anything could happen.”

Speaking on Monday’s Club Random, Maher explained Trump’s latest peace offering, sharing text exchanges between himself and the president.

“Then, like, he just, out of the blue, `Let’s have dinner again.’ I was like, ‘great.’ And he was really nice. Like, `I promise I won’t say bad things about you like I did the last time.’ And I texted back, and I said, ‘You know what, you’re the president of the United States. Say whatever the f--- you want’.”

Maher added, “I’m just glad we’re talking.’ It’s like being called a ‘hockey puck’ by Don Rickles. It’s just what he does. It’s how he talks.”

Emanuel suggested to Maher, “There are some people you won’t talk to, there’s some people I won’t talk to.”

Maher said, “Yeah, but they’re not the president of the United States.”

The comedian added, “It blows my mind that there are people in this world, and lots of them on the far left, who just would turn this opportunity down, a private dinner, in the White House, with the president, just a few people, say whatever you want.”

Maher continued, “I’ve heard people say ‘I don’t like the war...’ Tell him! You can tell him. And I will. I keep telling people, he needs more people like us, not less.”

As the two men kept discussing their interactions with the president, Maher said, “There’s a way to talk to Donald Trump. There just is.”

Maher said after he shared details of their first dinner, he was told he was “humanizing” Trump by critics.

“OK, he’s a human,” Maher said. “I get it, he’s a very flawed one, as are we all under Jesus.”

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

 From partner draw to 5- truck fleet —NCB SME Fund fuels Maragh’s haulage growth 







KINGSTON, Jamaica – When 32-year-old entrepreneur Romario Maragh decided to start his trucking business in 2018, it was a ‘partner draw’ that helped him buy his first used truck.

Today, Ashmar’s Trucking & Haulage operates five trucks, moving containers and other cargo from Jamaica’s ports to customers across the island. NCB has financed the trucks that have supported the expansion of the business, including one acquired through the first NCB SME Growth Fund.

Now, Maragh is looking to add another truck to his fleet through the $2 billion NCB SME Growth Fund II.

“When an entrepreneur comes to us for financing, the real question is what that financing will allow the business to do next,” said Perrin Gayle, executive vice president, Retail Banking at National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCB).

“For Maragh, another truck means greater capacity to serve his customers and pursue more business. That is what we want the SME Growth Fund to facilitate, giving viable Jamaican businesses access to the capital they need to take their next step.”

Launched in April 2026, this second iteration of NCB’s SME Growth Fund received more than 2,000 applications from businesses seeking financing within the first two months. To date, just over $2.048 billion in loans have been identified within the approved SME Growth Fund II rate bands.

Trucking runs in Maragh’s family. His father operates a trucking business overseas, while his grandfather and stepfather were also involved in the industry. But when he established Ashmar’s Trucking & Haulage, he had to build the business for himself.

As the company expanded, his relationship with NCB Business Banker Tamara Spence became an even more important part of that journey.

Maragh recalled that securing financing was initially a learning experience, particularly around the financial records and business practices required. He credits Spence with helping him understand those requirements and prepare the business to access financing.

“When I see something I want to buy, she helps me to figure out the best way for me to get it,” he said. “She has played such a key role in helping my business to grow. I don’t know if I could have done as much without her.”

For Maragh, access to financing has also changed the type of equipment he is able to put into the business. Having started with a used truck, he now prioritises purchasing new, reliable equipment, which he says is critical in the haulage industry.

“When you’re in haulage, you need good, solid equipment because if the truck is down, you’re not working,” Maragh said. “Repairs can cost you up to J$5 million, and then you have the loss for the time that the truck is off the road as well. With the financing, I can get some of the best trucks on the market brand new, so I have better uptime and I’m not constantly spending on repairs.”

The support from Spence has also connected him with other services across NCB Financial Group. When the cost of insuring his growing fleet became a concern, Spence referred him to Guardian General Insurance Jamaica Limited. Maragh said the move helped him reduce his fleet insurance costs by more than 60 per cent.

“I complained to Tamara about the cost to insure the trucks, and she put me on to Guardian,” he recalled. “The discounted fleet rates they offer have made a big difference for the business.”

For Maragh, having access to the right financing and financial support has made it possible to pursue the ambitions he has for Ashmar’s Trucking & Haulage.

“Facilities like NCB’s SME Fund are truly helpful for businesses that want to grow. So many people have ambition and big dreams, but just need some solid financial backing to bring these to life,” he said.

The $2 billion facility followed NCB’s first $1 billion SME Growth Fund, which was fully taken up. The allocation was doubled for the second fund, providing greater access to financing for SMEs seeking to invest in their businesses.

Sheree Martin, chief executive officer of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited, said the response to the faund points to the ambition of Jamaica’s SME community and the importance of ensuring viable businesses can access financing to pursue their plans.

“Behind every application is a business owner with a plan, whether that is to purchase equipment, increase capacity, enter a new market, take on a larger contract or strengthen the business they have already built. The response to the SME Growth Fund tells us that Jamaican entrepreneurs are ready to invest in their businesses. Our role is to continue finding practical ways to help them access the financing and financial guidance they need to move those plans forward,” Martin said.

news.title: PM Modi's free trade push could lead to $140 billion GDP gain for India
news.text:
ET OnlineAs countries redraw supply chains around trusted partners and seek preferential market access, New Delhi has ended years of caution and is rapidly expanding its free-trade network. (AI-generated image)

A more protectionist US could prove an unexpected tailwind for India’s economy. As countries redraw supply chains around trusted partners and seek preferential market access, New Delhi has ended years of caution and is rapidly expanding its free-trade network.Using a large-scale model of the global economy developed by the World Trade Organization, we estimate these agreements could add about $140 billion to India’s GDP in 2035, opening new markets, cutting import costs, fostering foreign direct investment and lifting productivity.We also consider two scenarios that could amplify the gains: realizing further productivity benefits from a decade of reforms to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, and enacting policies that help underemployed agricultural workers transition into manufacturing and services.ALSO READ | India’s billion-dollar trade juggernaut has an unwanted case of missing balanceLive EventsThe Great Redrawing of Global Trade MapsThe surge in US tariffs since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 is redrawing global trade links. After 19 months of wild swings, we estimate the average US tariff rate stood at 10.7% in August, up from 2.3% in 2024. That reflects sectoral tariffs—mainly on cars and metals, and country-specific levies set at around 10%-12.5% under the Section 301 forced labor action. Tariffs at this rate could lower US goods imports by roughly 15% compared with the previous regime. Threats and investigations point to more hikes to come.Other countries are responding by diversifying trade links and accelerating negotiations with new partners. Since the start of 2025, the European Union has signed new or updated agreements with Mercosur and Mexico and concluded negotiations with Indonesia, India and Australia. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China signed an upgraded free-trade agreement in October 2025. Canada signed several agreements in 2025-26 and moved to launch, accelerate or revive others.ALSO READ | New FTAs open big export gains across key sectorsIndia is no exception. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association, the UK and Oman entered into force, adding to deals with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022. India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations with the EU. In addition, New Delhi is pursuing other partners—including the Eurasian Economic Union—and has sought an agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.At the same time, India has pursued deeper trade links with the US since Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced plans for a bilateral agreement in February 2025. The relationship has been rocky. In the second half of 2025, India faced some of the highest additional tariffs among major US trading partners after Washington imposed a 25% reciprocal tariff and an additional 25% duty linked to Russian oil purchases.Tensions have eased since then. While sectoral tariffs remain in place, the US removed the Russia-related 25% tariff and lowered reciprocal rates on India to 18% in February. In addition, under the Section 301 forced labor action, which has replaced reciprocal tariffs, India has been set a rate of 10%, lower than the 12.5% slapped on many other partners. This is paving the way for an interim deal, though reaching a more comprehensive agreement may prove difficult.What Trade Reshuffling Means for the Indian EconomyUsing a computable general equilibrium model, we estimate how India’s trade deals could reshape its economy over the next decade.We start by assessing the impact of US tariffs at their August level, relative to 2024 duties. We calculate that the average tariff on Indian goods sold to the US has risen to 11.6%, from 2.4% in 2024. By 2035, we estimate the tariffs will cut Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth. But the hit to India’s economy should be limited. Less than 2% of its output relies on US markets, and stronger exports elsewhere should cushion the blow. We estimate the effect on gross domestic product will be negligible.We then model the FTAs already concluded or under negotiation through three channels:First, we adjust bilateral tariffs using a stylized schedule that captures the key elements of the deals. India’s partners eliminate all tariffs on Indian goods in the first year. India eliminates tariffs on industrial products and halves those on agricultural products, implementing half of the reduction in the first year and the rest by year 10.Second, building on Metivier et al. (2023), we assume the cost of nontariff measures on goods and services falls gradually by 25% over 15 years, with an additional reduction in NTMs on services to capture lower uncertainty from bilateral agreements.Third, using Prasad et al. (2008), we add a productivity boost from higher FDI in line with commitments under the deals: $100 billion over 15 years for EFTA (roughly $35 billion of which is expected to be additional), and $20 billion for New Zealand (almost all additional).For US-India negotiations, we model an interim agreement under which India grants the US roughly the same tariff reductions as under its other deals. The US cuts sectoral duties on automotive products to 15% (including most-favored-nation tariffs) but keeps the 50% metal tariffs and 10% Section 301 duties on most covered products—similar to the conditions it granted other deal partners such as the EU or Japan. We still expect the agreement to reduce tensions and uncertainty and to deliver the same decline in NTMs as India’s other FTAs.Our analysis suggests FTAs already in force should raise India’s GDP by 1.2% by 2035 relative to baseline, rising to 1.7% if the EU and New Zealand agreements are implemented from 2027, a gain of about $140 billion at constant 2025 US dollars. A US deal would add 0.2 percentage point. If negotiations with the EAEU, GCC and Israel conclude over the next few years, the gain could rise by another 0.2 ppt, leaving GDP 2.1% higher (about $170 billion) by 2035.Trade volumes would rise even faster. By 2035, Indian exports could be almost 10% above baseline if all deals are implemented. Imports also would climb as households and businesses gain access to new products and services and manufacturers become more integrated into global value chains.How Domestic Trends Could Compound the BoostSigning FTAs is only the first step. Reaping the full benefits will require India to sustain its reform momentum. Effective implementation; reliable access to energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies; and unlocking the potential of India’s vast labor force will all be important.We model an upside scenario in which two domestic trends amplify the gains:Lower production costs. India has cut corporate taxes, introduced subsidies, ramped up infrastructure investment to lower logistics costs and funded incentives to boost workers’ skills. Regardless of trade developments, some of these benefits likely have already materialized. In this upside scenario we assume a further boost to manufacturers’ efficiency, which we model as a roughly 2% decline in production costs. That could add roughly 1 ppt to export gains and 0.5 ppt to GDP gains by 2035.Tap India’s agricultural labor potential. More than 40% of Indian workers remain in agriculture—little changed over the past decade—with high underemployment. By comparison, in rapidly industrializing Vietnam the share has fallen from more than 40% to around 25%, while agricultural output per worker has risen rapidly and now exceeds India’s by almost 60%. We model a similar productivity boost in India phased in over a decade, allowing workers to shift toward expanding manufacturing and services. This adds slightly more than 1 ppt to export growth and about 2 ppts to GDP gains.India is pairing an ambitious industrial strategy with an equally ambitious trade agenda. If it gets the combination right, it could become a powerful new engine of long-term growth. US tariffs are a drag. For India, and the world, the right response could yet deliver a development win.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.

Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.

“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”

When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”

The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.

“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.

Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.

Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law. Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.

But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.

“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”

Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.

“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.

“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.

The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.

Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.

An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.

Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.

“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

news.title: Trump attacks immigrants from Somalia and Haiti while rallying in Ohio for Republican candidates
news.text:
COLUMBUS: President Donald Trump on Monday tried to boost Sen. Jon Husted’s reelection campaign by attacking two groups of Black immigrants during a rally in Ohio, where an organization with Republican ties began promoting a socialist candidate over Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown.

Trump also gave a shoutout to Rep. Max Miller, the Republican congressman who refused to stop running for reelection after facing accusations of domestic abuse, pointing him out in the audience.

“Thank you, Max, for coming,” Trump said. “Thank you. Very good.”

Trump focused, however, on a favorite issue — immigration. Trump has long targeted Minnesota’s large population of Somali immigrants and on Monday he linked that group to Haitians in Springfield, Ohio. During a presidential debate two years ago, Trump falsely accused the latter group of eating pets. Referencing those allegations Monday, Trump said “I was right” and boasted that Haitians were being driven out of the country by his administration’s policies.

“If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota is being destroyed, we’re going to stop it,” Trump said. “Just like we did with Springfield, we’re going to stop it, we’re not going to let it happen.”

Trump’s remarks came on the same day Homeland Security agents searched the Washington home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Somali immigrant who represents a Minnesota district.

The president visited Youngstown less than a week after rallying in Dayton. The intense focus on Ohio, a state Trump won by 11 percentage points, shows the challenging environment Republicans are navigating in the midterms amid the Iran war and lingering inflation. In addition to the Senate contest, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a close governor’s race with Democrat Amy Acton.

The rally was also a reminder of the extent Trump is willing to go to boost his allies — he announced a new submarine component manufacturing center will be located in nearby Cleveland during the rally — and his persistent focus on Black immigrants.

Back in 2018, Trump privately complained about immigrants from countries like Haiti — using an expletive to describe them — and wondering why the United States couldn’t get more migrants from places like Norway. The statement was condemned as racist and Trump denied making it at the time.

But Trump admitted using the phrase last year, and his second administration has focused on restricting immigration and barring any refugees except white South Africans.

During the rally, he celebrated what he contended was an exodus of Haitians out of Springfield. The Trump administration ended a program that allowed more than 350,000 Haitians to stay in the country legally, which some of the roughly 15,000 Haitians who arrived in Springfield, population 60,000, in recent years.

“They’re getting their town back,” Trump said about the original residents of Springfield, as he also stood by his debunked statement at the 2024 presidential debate that the Haitians were eating local pets. That claim was based on a secondhand Facebook post whose author deleted it and apologized, saying she had no evidence it was true.

Trump devoted even more time to insulting immigrants from Somalia, where he claimed that people were “low IQ” and “don’t have pants to wear.”

Trump’s main goal was to boost Husted, who was appointed to replace Vice President JD Vance in the Senate in 2024 and faces a tough challenge from Brown, a longtime senator who lost his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.

The presidential visit came after mailers, sponsored by Enough Promises Ohio PAC, began arriving in voters’ mailboxes in recent days. They promote independent candidate Greg Levy over Brown with messages such as “Join the Revolution” and “Send a Worker to the Senate.” Levy describes himself as “Socialist running for the US Senate to represent Ohio in 2026” on his X account.

Levy condemned the fliers for falsely impersonating his campaign and engaging in “dirty tricks” designed to mislead voters. He said he is considering legal action.

“This is a highly undemocratic practice and does a disservice to voters in Ohio and throughout the country,” he wrote on X.

According to Federal Election Commission filings, Enough Promises Ohio was founded Sept. 29. It has not yet had to disclose its contributors, but additional federal filings lay out a trail of associations linked to Republicans.

Enough Promises paid the firm Seven Farms more than $397,000 on two dates last week for printing, postage and mail services either supporting Levy or opposing Brown. Seven Farms, also a new entity, lists as its address the same South Carolina business suite as the one used by Whistlestop Strategies LLC.

Whistlestop is a direct mail outfit operated by Big Dog Strategies LLC, the strategy firm that advises Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC and that managed Moreno’s successful campaign against Brown in 2024.

Enough Promises Ohio and Big Dog did not respond to requests for comment.

 US actress Selma Blair arrested after flight altercation 







NEW YORK, United States (AFP)—United States (US) actress Selma Blair was arrested after an alleged altercation on a flight from Los Angeles to New York City that injured at least two cabin crew members, authorities said Monday.

The “Legally Blonde” and “Cruel Intentions” star was detained at John F Kennedy Airport after her Delta Air Lines flight landed late Sunday following reports of a physically abusive passenger.

US media said that Blair punched one flight attendant and bit another. The 54-year-old then reportedly assaulted a police officer and nurse as she was transported to hospital.

“Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct,” a representative for Blair said.

“Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

The FBI issued a summons accusing Blair of assaults on the plane, according to a federal judicial source.

A spokesperson for Delta said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.”

In 2016, Blair was removed from a plane on a stretcher after another outburst on a flight.

“I mixed alcohol with medication, and that caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” she told Vanity Fair after that incident.

She also described in her 2022 memoir having bitten several celebrities, including Kate Moss, often in situations where she had been drinking alcohol.

October 12, 2026




 Sangster International named Caribbean’s Leading Airport at World Travel Awards 

Montego Bay facility extends winning streak to 18 consecutive years 






ST JAMES, Jamaica — Less than a year after Hurricane Melissa forced its closure, Sangster International Airport (SIA) has been named the Caribbean’s Leading Airport 2026 by the World Travel Awards (WTA). 

The award, presented at the WTA Caribbean & The Americas Gala Ceremony at Princess Grand Jamaica, on Sunday, extends the airport’s winning streak to 18 consecutive years and brings its total to 19 titles.

The recognition comes weeks before the first anniversary of the Category 5 hurricane – the strongest ever to make landfall in Jamaica on October 28, 2025.

“Last October, we were navigating a very challenging, life-changing period in the aftermath of the hurricane. This October, we are accepting the region’s leading airport award,” said Shane Munroe, Chief Executive Officer of MBJ Airports Limited (MBJ), in a press release. “We accept this unprecedented honour with great humility, especially after being able to quickly restore the facilities and experience for passengers after Hurricane Mellissa. This is a result of the incredible collaborative work done by all members of our Team Sangster family – our team, our airlines, government agencies and the partners who stood with us.”

SIA handles over 70 percent of Jamaica’s passengers, and its reopening was central to restarting the tourism economy in Montego Bay and surrounding parishes. Since the storm, MBJ has worked with airline partners to restore and grow service, with 26 airlines now serving 47 destinations, the operator said in the release.

It added that, over the past year, MBJ’s commitment to growing air service connectivity has been reflected in several key route developments, including Wingo Airlines’ services from Bogotá and Medellín, Colombia; Flair Airlines from Toronto; and WestJet from Québec City and Montréal, Canada. These additions strengthen Jamaica’s air connectivity with Canada and South America, creating new opportunities for tourism, trade and regional travel.

Additional services are scheduled to commence before the end of 2026, further strengthening SIA’s route network. These include Porter Airlines’ services from Hamilton, Ottawa, and London, Canada; and Breeze Airways from Tampa, Florida. These new connections will broaden travel options between Jamaica, Canada and the United States while supporting continued market diversification and growth.

Through strategic collaboration with airline partners and tourism stakeholders, MBJ said it remains

committed to expanding airlift, strengthening international access and positioning Sangster

International Airport as a leading gateway to Jamaica and a vital link to the wider world.

“Visitors can’t return without airlift, and every flight we brought back was crucial for hotels,

attractions, transport operators and small businesses,” Munroe highlighted. “SIA is the main gateway

to Jamaica, so reconnecting Jamaica to its markets was our first priority.”

Before the storm, MBJ outlined several transformation projects including the expansion of the check

in area, Immigration Hall, East Concourse, parking and outbound security, alongside the

implementation of full biometric processing on departures.Munroe stated that all projects were

back on track with the Caribbean’s Leading Airport looking to deliver the next level of excellence to

its users. 

Sharon Hislop-Holt, Manager, Commercial Business Development and Marketing at MBJ, said the

award reflects the team members’ steady commitment to supporting their passengers and one another. 

“We have very dedicated team members who take a lot of pride in serving our passengers.This was

demonstrated throughout the year and came to the fore after the hurricane.Even as staff dealt with

loss or damage to their own homes, they showed up for work and made certain that every passenger

who walked through our doors was cared for,” said Hislop-Holt. 

That support also reached neighbouring communities. The MBJ Foundation presented J$30 million

in grants from its 2025 Charity Run/Walk to 184 secondary and tertiary students from western

Jamaica and three institutions.

According to the release, J$15 million of the proceeds was earmarked for rebuilding hurricane

damaged schools, supported by additional funds from MBJ’s shareholders, Grupo Aeroportuario del

Pacífico (GAP) and Vantage Airport Group.

Munroe said the airport’s responsibility now is to “continue living up to the recognition while

enhancing the Caribbean’s leading gateway.To every member of our airport community, thank you.”

 ‘Breaking Bad’ actor RJ Mitte dead at 34 







LOS ANGELES, United States (AFP)—RJ Mitte, the young actor best known for playing Walter White Jr in the award-winning TV series Breaking Bad, has died, his representatives told AFP on Monday. He was 34.

The cause of death for the actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, was not immediately revealed.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” said a statement issued by Sean Reilly.

A teenage Mitte first appeared in Breaking Bad in 2008 as the son of chemistry-teacher-turned-drug-kingpin Walter White, a role that won Bryan Cranston global acclaim.

“Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” Reilly said.

That campaigning evolved into working as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and for Shriners Children’s, a non-profit hospital network.

“He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities,” Reilly added.

Breaking Bad, which ran for five seasons between 2008 and 2013, is routinely acclaimed as groundbreaking television and was named by The New York Times as the best TV show of the 21st century.

news.title: ASX 200 Pares Midday Losses as Oil Surge, Gold Slide and Tech Sell-Off Test Australian Shares on Tuesday
news.text: SYDNEY — Australian shares recovered much of their early-session slide on Tuesday afternoon, though the benchmark index remained slightly lower as rising oil prices, a stronger U.S. dollar and a broad technology sell-off weighed on sentiment.The S&P/ASX 200 was down 13.1 points, or 0.15%, at 8,770.1 as of 2:13 p.m. Sydney time, well above its midday level. By lunchtime, the index had fallen 41.7 points, or 0.47%, to 8,741.7, while the broader All Ordinaries had dropped 46.7 points, or 0.53%, to 8,890.3.The afternoon rebound trimmed roughly two-thirds of the index's midday losses, but the market was still handing back part of Monday's rally. The ASX 200 had closed Monday at 8,783.2, up 66.6 points, or 0.76%.Oil and the dollar set the toneThe pullback followed a mixed overnight session on global markets, with higher oil prices and continuing uncertainty over the outlook for artificial intelligence weighing on risk appetite, Westpac economist Neha Sharma said."Energy markets remained the key focus," Sharma said, pointing to doubts over U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and concerns about fuel availability that reinforced expectations of prolonged supply disruptions. She added that the U.S. dollar strengthened alongside oil, while the Australian dollar and most major currencies weakened against the greenback.Brent crude was trading at $105.70 a barrel after climbing above $107 overnight to its highest level of October. The spike came as U.S. lawmakers from both major parties criticized Trump's Russian diesel supply deal and as fighting between Saudi forces and Houthi rebels continued.The Australian dollar was buying 69.53 U.S. cents, down from 69.77 U.S. cents at 5 p.m. Monday.Miners and gold stocks dragThe combination of higher oil prices and a firmer U.S. dollar hit the local resources sector, which is heavily weighted in the benchmark. The materials sector fell 1.7% by midday, with BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue all trading lower.That marked a sharp reversal from Monday, when materials stocks led gains in midday trading as gold, silver and copper prices edged higher, with BHP up 3% and Rio Tinto rising more than 1% at that stage.Gold miners also came under pressure. The precious metal slumped to $4,165 an ounce, pulling the gold sub-index down 1.7%.Energy and consumer stocks provide supportEnergy shares were among the few bright spots, benefiting directly from the oil rally. Santos, Woodside and Ampol each rose more than 1.4%, while coal producers were mixed. Uranium stocks sold off after enthusiasm around artificial intelligence, a key driver of demand expectations for nuclear power, faded overnight.Consumer-facing stocks bounced back after a soft start to the week. Consumer staples gained 0.8% and consumer discretionary shares rose 0.4%.Financials edged higher, helped by modest gains in the big four banks and major insurers, though Macquarie and most other financial services companies slipped. The banking sector's steadiness was important for the broader market, given its heavy weighting in the index. Financial shares had surged 1.56% on Monday, leading the market higher.Tech worst performerTechnology was the weakest sector by lunchtime, sliding 2.4% in a broad sell-off that followed the Nasdaq's overnight decline. The losses reflected a wider reassessment of the artificial intelligence trade that has buffeted global technology stocks in recent sessions.The sell-off was a reversal from Monday, when the local technology index rose 0.85%.Telstra under pressure at AGMAmong individual stocks, Telstra shares fell 0.7% to 4.62 Australian dollars as management faced shareholders at the company's annual general meeting. Chief Executive Vicki Brady offered a fresh apology for the nationwide outage in July.The stock has fallen almost 5% in less than three sessions. Telstra shares had already slid 3% in midday trading Monday, extending losses from Friday.The July outage, caused by a critical software fault, halted train lines and disrupted business transactions. It was the third major national outage in less than a year for the company, which supports about 25 million Australian mobile services. At the time, Brady said the company had "let our customers and Australians down."Telstra faces potential civil penalties under powers the government introduced after the 2025 Optus outage.RBA keeps hike option openInvestors also weighed the Reserve Bank of Australia's September meeting minutes, released Tuesday. The minutes said Australia's inflation outlook would continue to be affected by developments in the Middle East and did not rule out further increases in the cash rate.The board said it would remain focused on its mandate of price stability and full employment and would do what it considered necessary to achieve that, including raising the cash rate target further if required.The prospect of additional tightening has hung over the market in recent weeks, as elevated energy costs feed into inflation expectations. Higher interest rates typically weigh on equity valuations, particularly for growth-oriented sectors such as technology.Index below recent highsTuesday's level leaves the benchmark about 5.7% below its 52-week high of 9,296.7. The index's 52-week low of 8,262.4 was set on March 23.The market has been choppy in recent weeks as investors balance strong commodity prices against concerns about inflation, interest rates and the impact of the Middle East conflict on global growth.On Monday, buy now, pay later provider Zip topped the ASX 200 leaderboard, closing 5.56% higher at 2.28 Australian dollars, ahead of its first-quarter trading update scheduled for Oct. 23.What's aheadMarket watchers will be looking to overnight trading on Wall Street, movements in crude oil and gold, and any further developments in the Middle East for direction heading into Wednesday's session.Investors will also be monitoring commodity prices closely, given the heavy influence of miners on the benchmark index, as well as further signals from the Reserve Bank on the path of interest rates.The Australian sharemarket closes at 4 p.m. Sydney time.

news.title: Trump, 80, Thirsts Over ‘Beautiful’ MAGA Barbie, 30
news.text:
President Donald Trump has thirsted over a “beautiful” WNBA player during a midterm campaign rally in Ohio on Monday.

Trump, 80, mentioned Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, 30, by name at the rally. Cunningham earned the nickname “MAGA Barbie” during her college days in Missouri, reportedly due to following conservatives including Candice Owens online, according to Complex.

She became a polarizing figure in the WNBA after an ESPN profile in July in which she stated that she advocated against the inclusion of transgender athletes in women’s sports to “protect women’s sports.” 

Despite her professional success, Trump suggested male sports fans had another motivation to watch her play.

“We like Sophie Cunningham. You have a lot of men wanting to go and watch her. She’s beautiful,” Trump said of Cunningham. 

“You’re not allowed to say that anymore, however, as a politician. Please, please, let me take it back. Anytime a politician says a woman is beautiful, that’s generally the end of his political career in the modern-day politic world.”

“But Sophie is a beautiful young woman,” he added. “You probably wouldn’t mind her on the team, not to help you with points, but to help you with attendance. The attendance would be great.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House for comment.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

news.title: ‘They Agreed Because I Said They Agreed’ – Trump Insists Ukraine, Russia Accepted Energy Ceasefire Despite Denials
news.text:
US President Donald Trump insisted Monday, Oct. 12, that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure simply because he told them to, despite neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirming any agreement and Russian strikes continuing against Ukrainian facilities.

Speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for Ohio, Trump was challenged over his announcement of an energy ceasefire the previous day, which appeared to catch both governments by surprise.

“They agreed. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ – that’s why,” Trump replied.

“They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled,” he added.

The exchange followed Trump’s Sunday announcement that the two countries had agreed to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure immediately, although he provided no details about the arrangement or how it would be enforced.

Trump questions reports of Russian ceasefire violations

Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities after his announcement, Trump said he was uncertain whether Moscow had violated the supposed agreement.

“I’m not sure about that,” he said, before urging both leaders to bring the war to an end.

Trump also suggested that violations had occurred on both sides, without providing evidence or identifying specific incidents.

When reporters pressed him on whether Russian President Vladimir Putin had actually accepted the proposal, Trump insisted that both leaders supported the idea.

“I think they both support it. I think they wanna make a deal, but they don’t know how. But we’re gonna get them to make a deal,” he said.

He then suggested Putin was more willing to negotiate than President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky,” Trump said.

Zelensky says Russian strikes continue despite Trump’s announcement

Earlier Monday, Zelensky said Russian forces had attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s announcement, including a power plant in Kharkiv and a gas-production facility.

Speaking by video link at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had refrained from striking Russian refineries overnight, but Moscow had not reciprocated.

Ukraine was ready to observe an energy ceasefire if Russia did the same, he said, urging Washington to ensure Moscow complied with any agreement.

In his official address, Zelensky said Russian drone attacks continued over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities after Trump’s declaration.

The Kremlin had not confirmed accepting Trump’s proposal, and no jointly agreed ceasefire terms or monitoring arrangements had been announced.

Trump defends diesel deal with Moscow

Trump’s insistence that an energy ceasefire was in place came amid growing criticism of his administration’s agreement to allow Russian diesel exports.

Announced after a conversation with Putin on Friday, Oct. 9, the arrangement temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel imports as Washington sought to relieve pressure on fuel prices.

The decision drew objections from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who warned that additional energy revenues could help finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Trump defended the arrangement Monday, arguing that European governments continued purchasing Russian energy while criticizing Washington’s decision.

A bipartisan group of seven US senators had urged the administration to reverse course, warning against providing Moscow with additional financial resources while Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians continued.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump insisted Monday, Oct. 12, that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire because he told them to, despite neither government confirming such a deal. Trump dismissed questions about continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and claimed Putin was more eager to reach a peace agreement than Zelensky. His remarks came amid growing controversy over Washington’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

news.title: 'Government that works': Third parties, independents fight midterms and the US system
news.text: WASHINGTON: Three's a crowd in US elections where in next month's midterms assorted outliers ranging from Libertarians to Greens will try vainly to break the Democratic-Republican grip on the system.Hundreds of third-party candidates are standing in the November 3 contest for the House of Representatives and Senate. But to the growing frustration of voters wanting to disrupt the status quo they have no chance of beating the Democrats and Republicans. "Why am I standing? I ask myself that every morning," admits Tim Sharman, who is running as an independent for Virginia's 8th District seat in the House."I don't feel I belong in the Democratic Party, nor in the Republican Party. So I thought, let's have a go at shaking it up."I come with a business background, so I believe in solutions and collaboration across the spectrum."Sharman, 62, spent $40,000 on his push to gather the 1,000 verified signatures required to get on the ballot for the midterms.He relies on friends for logistical support in his one-man campaign under the slogan "Government that works. Politics that doesn't get in the way.""Actually running for office has been fun and engaging," he said."If you met me in a bar a year ago, I'd have opinions, but when you have to think through policy positions, it's a lot harder because there's always trade-offs, which has been an interesting exercise.".Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the US midterm elections?.Drift from main parties?A record high 45 percent of US adults identified as independent in a Gallup survey released this year, pointing to growing dissatisfaction at the Republican and Democratic parties that have had a stranglehold on power since the 1850s.Young people are much less likely to identify with either of the main two parties, the survey found, citing 56 percent of Gen Z-ers saying they were independent.For Dianne Blais, standing for Congress as a Green Party candidate is not about winning but about continuing her work as a volunteer that ranges from serving in school positions to fostering children."I'm so unhappy and upset about what's happening in this country, and this is one thing I know how to do," said Blais, who has run for the Greens before.She first joined the party to promote rail transport to ease road congestion, and now describes herself as primarily a peace activist, criticizing both Democratic former president Joe Biden and Republican President Donald Trump for failing to halt wars worldwide."I just hope to educate a few people," she said.Blais cites Green candidate Ralph Nader, who won three percent of the national vote in 2000, as a major inspiration for the third-party movement -- though Ross Perot pulled in a huge 19 percent as an independent in 1992."The way the system is, there's just no winning when you're a third party," she said.US elections are almost all winner-take-all contests, meaning a party that wins 15 percent or more of the vote nationwide can end up with nothing, and no Libertarian or Green has ever been elected to Congress..Nine US states have new House districts for midterm elections after Trump urged changes.Knocking on doorsBlais, 72, has avoided door-to-door campaigning this year due to aggressive dogs -- in contrast to Libertarian Party candidate Taner Lopez, 46, who has been pressing the flesh at every opportunity."I have weekly breakfasts, we have a tent at events like agricultural fairs," he told news.title: Both parties court Indian Americans in Michigan battleground
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 13 (IANS) Republicans and Democrats in Michigan are openly courting Indian-American voters three weeks before the November 3 midterms, with the state Republican Party claiming community backing for Senate nominee Mike Rogers and Democrats pitching the prospect of an Indian-American Speaker of the state House. The Michigan Republican Party said in a post on X on Sunday night that "The Indian-American community in Michigan is coming out big-time for Mike Rogers and our entire Republican ticket.” The post, billed as a live update from the field in Oakland County, named Michigan GOP Co-Chair Sunny Reddy and Republican National Committee National Committeewoman Hima Kolanagireddy, both Indian Americans, as among those at the event. The party did not give figures on turnout or voter support for its claim. Hours earlier, a Democratic state House campaign, posting as @HaleyforMI, said Democrats were "about to flip the state house and make Ranjeev Puri THE FIRST! Indian American State House Speaker in the country!” Puri, a Democrat from Canton in Wayne County, has been House Democratic Leader since January 2025. He represents the 24th District and is on the ballot for re-election. Republicans currently control the Michigan House under Speaker Matt Hall, while Democrats hold the state Senate and the governorship. Puri would become Speaker only if Democrats win a House majority and his caucus elects him to the post. A review of state legislative leadership records found no Indian American who has served as Speaker of a state House or Assembly. Indian Americans have held senior posts below that level, including Upendra Chivukula and Raj Mukherji, both deputy speakers in the New Jersey General Assembly. After the August 4 primary, Puri said House Democrats' mission was "to take back the Michigan House, restore our Democratic trifecta, and keep our state moving forward.” The outreach comes as the Senate race between Rogers, a former Republican congressman, and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has turned bitter. At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Monday night, President Donald Trump attacked El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants. "You look at the guy running in Michigan. He's a jihadist," Trump said. Trump had also called El-Sayed a "radical jihadist" at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee on Saturday, and has repeatedly referred to him as "Mohammed" rather than Abdul. "He knows my name is Abdul. He says it every day. But he's not just attacking me. He's attacking all of us," El-Sayed said in response on X. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate. Neither post offered details of Indian-American voter registration or turnout in Michigan, and neither campaign has released polling on the community's preferences. Michigan has a sizable Indian-American population concentrated in the Detroit suburbs, including Oakland County and Canton Township. The state was one of the narrowest battlegrounds in the 2024 presidential election, and the Senate seat is open following the retirement of Democrat Gary Peters. Indian Americans have traditionally leaned Democratic, though Republicans have sought to make inroads in recent cycles, fielding a growing number of community candidates and appointing community leaders to party posts.

news.title: Professor accused of soaking student’s backpack in urine admits to disturbing habit
news.text:
The science professor has been charged with one count of first-degree damage to property

A US college professor is facing a felony charge after being accused of soaking a student’s back in pee.

Science professor Paul Fischer, 55, is accused of causing more than $2,000 worth of damage after soaking the backpack in his own urine, court documents show.

Fischer, who taught at Macalester College in Minnesota for more than 25 years, has been charged with one count of first-degree damage to property.

If he is convicted, Fischer could be given up to five-years in prison and a maximum fine of $10,000.

In the complaint, which was filed at the Ramsey County Attorney’s Office last week, the student said she left her backpack unattended at Macalester’s science block for around five minutes or so on 5 December 2025.

But when she returned she noticed the bag was damp and was horrified to discover what she believed to be ‘urine on her backpack’.

The unnamed student told cops that she believed the professor was the culprit as she’d been near his office and he was the only other person in the area at the time.

The student claimed that the incident resulted in her belongings being damaged and provided receipts totalling around $2,070 for the items that were ruined.

Following the complaint from the student, officers from St Paul police contacted the Macalester College Department of Public Safety and was told that ‘an investigation had been conducted, and it was discovered that an individual had been caught urinating around campus and that the individual resigned pending the investigation’.

The individual was identified as Fischer, the complaint said.

The Macalester College Department of Public Safety claimed that between 11 November and 5 December, there had been six reports of urination happening at the campus’ Olin-Rice Science Center and ‘included urine located in trash cans, individuals’ water bottles, and inside other professors’ decorations’, TwinCities reports.

Speaking to police, Fischer reportedly admitted that he had ‘developed a habit’ of ‘urinating in a cup’ and then disposing of the waste around the college’s campus in rubbish bins or lab sinks.

He said that on 5 December, he was emptying one such container of urine into a bin near his office, which was situated near the desk the student had been using.

Fischer told police that he believed the cup of urine may have spilled onto her belongings.

In a statement shared with CBS News, a spokesperson for Macalester College said: “Macalester College is aware of the criminal charge against Paul Fischer.

"Fischer's employment with Macalester ended during the 2025–26 academic year.”

Fischer is due to attend a court appearance over the matter early next month.

news.title: Trump hails Ramaswamy as 'very good friend', calls rival 'total lunatic'
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 13 (IANS) US President Donald Trump made a personal pitch for Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, calling his former primary rival a "very good friend" and branding his Democratic opponent Amy Acton a "total lunatic". Addressing supporters at the Covelli Centre, Trump recalled the 2024 Republican presidential primary, in which Ramaswamy ran against him before dropping out and endorsing him. "And we're going to send my very good friend -- you know, I ran against him, and he was not easy. He's a very smart guy and he's a very good guy. And he loves -- he loves this state," Trump said. "He's got a lot of great plans, like cutting taxes all over the place. You'll be very happy. You're going to be amazed at how good he is, how smart he is," he added. Trump turned sharply on Acton, a physician and former state health director. "Vivek is running against a total lunatic named Amy Acton, who shut down Ohio schools during Covid locked up your factories and your businesses," he said, adding that "she wants to take away your guns". He urged voters to back Ramaswamy and Senator Jon Husted. "If you want to stop it before it begins, vote for Jon Husted and vote for Vivek Ramaswamy," Trump said, after warning against Ohio being "plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota's being destroyed". "But this is, I think, about the only one I've made two. That means I like Ohio. We have to get Vivek -- And we have to get Jon," he said. Speaking before Trump took the stage, Ramaswamy said: "And I say this as the proud son of legal immigrants to this country your first act of entering this country cannot break the law that is why we are ending sanctuary cities in the state of Ohio.” "As Americans, we believe in merit, that the best person gets the job regardless of their skin color," he said, promising to be "the most conservative governor of this state has ever seen in our history". Joining Trump on stage later, Ramaswamy accused Acton of avoiding him, saying "the woman I'm running against actually refuses to show up for a debate with me". "I will be a governor who proudly works with the President of the United States of America to bring more dollars into Ohio, to bring higher paying jobs to Ohio," he said. Ramaswamy trails Acton by about four points in the MS NOW-FiftyPlusOne polling average. The election is on November 3. Ramaswamy, the Cincinnati-born son of immigrants from Kerala, would become the third Indian-American governor in US history, after Bobby Jindal of Louisiana and Nikki Haley of South Carolina, and the first from the Midwest. Republican incumbent Mike DeWine is term-limited.

SEOUL: South Korea’s ambassador to the United States said Washington had raised concerns about intelligence cooperation between the allies and that Seoul had not yet ​fully addressed US expectations, Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday.

news.text:
After Russia and Ukraine denied agreeing to the energy ceasefire, US President Donald Trump on Monday lashed out at reporters who pressed him about the basis of his announcement. He said that they had agreed to a ceasefire because he said so — irrespective of the reality on the ground.

But Trump has continued to blame Zelenskyy for the war and stressed on the need to end the war at any cost.
"That thing has to get settled. That war is a disaster. Did you see the numbers that just came out this month? 32,000, mostly soldiers, were killed. Young people, 32,000 killed. That war has to be over with," said Trump on Monday.

news.title: Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
news.text: Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude."Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, which has historically been its main source of revenue.In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.The new models can soon be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.Artificial Analysis's website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach $145 billion this year.The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world.-Speeding up- In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of "move fast and break things," but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed."Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would," Zuckerberg posted on X last month.In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping.At its annual developer conference Connect last month, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users' attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits.Zuckerberg sped up Muse's launch due to Instinct's popularity, the New York Times reported.Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models.Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged "pacing" - or slowing down - development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorization."We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month.
news.summary: Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
