news.title: Trump, once again, promises $5,000 payout to adult US citizens if Republicans win midterm elections
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) reiterated his promise to distribute cheques worth $5,000 to every adult citizen in the United States if Republicans secure control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, framing the potential payout as a direct outcome of Republican economic policies. 

Sharing a video message on Truth Social, Trump said, "I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000." He further accused democrats of planning to raise taxes, warning of "economic depression" if democrats win the elections. He, thus, presented his payout proposal as one of "economic success" in the country. 

"Democrat policies won't allow this to happen. In fact, the opposite—they're going to raise your taxes. If the Democrats win, you will have an economic depression. If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country like we have never ever seen before," he said. 

Earlier this month also, Trump promised to issue a $5,000 "dividend" to all adult citizens provided Republicans secure control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the upcoming 2026 midterm elections.In a video statement published on Truth Social, Trump framed the proposed $5,000 payout as an exclusive benefit of Republican leadership, claiming the federal government has generated record-setting revenues.

"Our country is doing so well under Republican leadership that only I can make you this promise. If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate, I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000, and Republicans can do it, and Democrats can't, because we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs and record-setting economic success," Trump said in the video message.

Warning voters of severe financial fallout if opposition parties prevail in the upcoming congressional elections, Trump cautioned that Democratic policies would wreck the economy: "But Democrat policies won't allow this to happen. In fact, the opposite is going to take place. They're going to raise your taxes and they're going to destroy our country and certainly destroy our economy. It'll be a 1929 disaster if they get in. So, if the Democrats win, you will have an economic depression, much like 1929. If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country, like we have never ever seen before."

Defending the feasibility of the plan, Trump pointed to previous financial distributions granted to armed service members as proof of his ability to execute large-scale direct payments. "And remember, just recently I gave all members of the military $1,776, just like 1776, and everyone said that was an impossible thing to do, but I did it, everybody got their money. I did it, and I'd do it again," Trump stated.

Citing vast capital inflows and national investment, Trump estimated the total cost of the direct checks at roughly $1 trillion. "The Trump dividend is approximately $1 trillion. But we have a record-setting $21 trillion that's being invested in our country in just the last 15 months, so it's actually a very easy thing to do for me, but the Democrats can never do it, because they never brought the goods and they never will. So, thank you, and I look forward to signing those checks."

Trump reinforced the announcement in an accompanying post caption, writing, "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 Midterm Elections, I’m going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America, $5,000!"

Similar assurance was given by Trump last month, as he promised a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” for every adult citizen, saying the payment “will happen” and linking it to the economic gains and revenue generated by the United States.

news.title: Trump Touts 'Big' Ohio Rally Crowd Size: What Videos, Pictures Show
news.text: President Donald Trump returned to Ohio on Monday for his second rally in the state in 10 days, touting the size of the crowd as he campaigned for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections. An energetic and lively audience filled the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, with local outlets reporting that rally-goers began lining up hours before doors opened. Some empty seats were also visible in footage from inside the venue. Hours before the rally, Trump said that a “big crowd” was expected in Ohio. “Tremendous Response to Radical Left Socialists, Communists, and Lunatics trying to take over our Country. See you later, Ohio!” Trump posted on Truth Social. Former NFL coach Jon Gruden introduced Trump, who took the stage for approximately 80 minutes—and was joined by Ohio Republican Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and YouTuber and professional boxer Jake Paul. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno spoke at the rally before Trump’s appearance. Embattled Ohio Republican Representative Max Miller was also in attendance, receiving a shoutout from Trump during his remarks. “Thank you, Max, for coming,” the president said. Trump's Monday appearance followed a rally in Vandalia on October 3. With Election Day just 22 days away, Ohio is a key battleground in the fight for control of the Senate and House. Husted is facing Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in a closely watched Senate race. What Videos and Pictures Show Videos from Monday's rally showed supporters gathered inside the Covelli Centre, with guests frequently responding to Trump's remarks with cheers and chants. The crowd repeatedly chanted "deport" during Trump's comments about immigration and Somali immigrants. Protesters who interrupted the president's speech also drew jeers from the audience. Several empty seats were visible in the venue. Videos and images provided a snapshot of the crowd and atmosphere but an official attendance figure has not been released. The Covelli Centre can accommodate up to 7,000 people, according to its website. Trump Targets Ilhan Omar and Somali Immigrants Trump repeatedly brought up Minnesota during his Ohio rally, directing criticism at Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, and the state's Somali community while discussing immigration and allegations of fraud. His remarks came several hours after federal agents searched Omar's home in Washington, D.C. The president addressed the search during the rally, distancing himself from the operation before criticizing the congresswoman. "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: She's a disaster," Trump said of Omar. Trump also attacked Somalia, where Omar was born, describing it as "one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet." He then turned his criticism toward Somali immigrants, prompting rally-goers to chant "deport" multiple times. Newsweek reached out to Omar's office for comment via email Monday night. Earlier Monday, Omar’s office condemned the raid as an “outrageous abuse of power.” “The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies,” her office wrote in a statement. The president has repeatedly invoked Minnesota in his criticism of alleged fraud involving members of the state's Somali community. The allegations have become a recurring feature of his broader attacks on immigration and Democratic-led states. Trump also invoked Minnesota as a warning to Ohio voters, arguing that Republicans must prevent their state from being "plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota." He urged voters to support Husted and Ramaswamy in next month's midterm elections. Protesters Interrupt Trump Protesters halted Trump's speech at multiple points, prompting boos from the crowd and angry responses from the president. As he has at previous rallies, Trump said the protesters were paid by the left. As one person was being escorted out, Trump told him to "go back home to mom" and called him a "fat guy." Trump also responded to another interruption by asking the crowd about the flag carried by a protester, wondering if it was Palestinian. Toward the end of his remarks, Trump brought up Paul, who grew up in Cleveland. “The protesters, do they not have jobs?” Paul said. “That's all they do—carry signs around while we do the work.” Trump is scheduled to continue his midterm campaign push Tuesday with a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, before holding rallies in Bullhead City, Arizona, and Kalispell, Montana, on Wednesday.  Black River ITA Service Hub to reopen October 13 







ST ELIZABETH, Jamaica —The Black River Service Hub of the Island Traffic Authority (ITA) is scheduled to reopen on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, and will resume services nearly a year after it was damaged along with much of the waterfront town by Hurricane Melissa.

news.title: Trump Hints at Possible Meeting With Kim Jong Un
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) said that there might be a possibility of meeting the Supreme Leader of North Korea, Kim Jong Un, during his upcoming Asia trip in mid-November and further expressed that the opportunity might be an “exciting one.”When asked about the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader, Trump told reporters, “I may…That’ll be exciting, won’t it? But I get along with him.” Trump had met Kim Jong Un three times during his first term as president.

Trump will be visiting China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting, which will take place in Shenzhen on November 18-19. The statement comes as earlier in August, US President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in the annual joint military exercises with South Korea, citing their cost, his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and concerns that the drills send an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to Pyongyang.

In a Truth Social post, Trump said he was unhappy that the United States had previously agreed to participate in the joint exercises with South Korea.”Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I was not happy with the fact that the United States had, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea,” Trump said.

“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” he added.

Trump said that since it was too late to cancel the exercises, he instructed US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to substantially reduce them.”Therefore, and based on the fact that it was too late to cancel, I instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump said.

Following the order, South Korea and the United States wrapped up their primary theatre-level combined military exercise on August 21, nearly a week ahead of schedule, Yonhap News Agency reported.The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise, typically an 11-day event involving command-post simulations and live field manoeuvres for contingencies on the Korean Peninsula, was halved to five days. The rollback has been widely viewed as a conciliatory gesture by Trump towards Kim Jong Un.

news.title: Trump defends Russia diesel deal as lawmakers from both parties complain
news.text:
ANIUS President Donald Trump has stood firm on a disputed diesel oil agreement with Russia

Washington: President Donald Trump on Monday defended a diesel oil deal he made with Russia as lawmakers from both parties complained the agreement appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.Trump has said the deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports would help bring down high fuel prices. However some analysts doubted the amount of diesel Trump has said Russia would provide over the next three months would do much to bring down prices, since it is equal to about 12 hours of global consumption of the fuel.On Friday, Trump said Russia had agreed to supply ​diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its ‌war on Ukraine. On Monday, Trump said the deal would help American farmers and ranchers.The price of diesel has surged more than 60% since Trump launched a war against Iran seven months ago, and high prices have jeopardized Republican chances to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.On Sunday a group of Republican and Democratic US senators called on Trump to "reverse course" on the diesel supply deal with Russia. They said his deal may violate a 2022 law designed to support Ukraine in its bid to repel Russian invaders.Live Events"We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them by allowing the import of Russian diesel and risking erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries," said Republican Senator Jerry Moran in a social media post.Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as a leading factor for higher diesel prices."I made the right choice for the American People - ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST! President DONALD J. TRUMP," Trump said in a social media post.On Monday, Trump rejected criticism of the deal from members of his own party, in comments to reporters as he departed the White House on a trip to Ohio."Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he said. "We can do a restriction on oil, but the rest of the world would be greatly, greatly affected if we do that."Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy bickered over the weekend about the Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Trump said Ukraine needs a new president and Zelenskiy promised to hold elections if Russia would agree to a 60-day ceasefire.Trump on Sunday declared that Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure. Whether such a deal will hold was unclear."Well, they agreed," Trump told reporters. "They agreed because I said they agreed. ... That war has to be over with."Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said contacts were proceeding about a possible energy ceasefire as announced by Trump. He declined to comment on whether the ceasefire would apply only to oil refineries.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv favoured a ceasefire, but both sides had to observe it. He said it was "increasingly clear" that Russia was unwilling to accept it as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy facilities on MondayZelenskiy told Fox News' "America's Newsroom"program on Monday that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries were not the leading cause of rising fuel prices."Everybody understands that the prices on diesel - it doesn't depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia. news.title: Oil ticks lower as Russia diesel supply prospects counter Gulf supply risks
news.text:
Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday after climbing by nearly $2 a barrel in ‌the previous session, as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia.

Brent crude futures fell 61 cents, or 0.57%, to $106.04 a barrel by 0000 GMT while US ​West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 47 cents, or 0.5%, at $93.27 a barrel.

Brent futures ​settled at $106.65 a barrel on Monday, the highest since September 15.

US President Donald ⁠Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US ​sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.

Additional supplies could help ​alleviate tightness in global fuel markets, tempering some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices recently.

However, lawmakers from both parties in the US complained Trump’s agreement with Putin appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ​energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.

“Fresh diesel supply from Russia and steadier Saudi flows ​are offering some relief, yet the market still looks more worried about the risk of further hits to ships ‌or ⁠pipelines in the Gulf than it is reassured by extra barrels,” Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said.

“Until we see clearer signs of de-escalation, the path of least resistance still leans higher,” he said.

Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck ​Riyadh’s international airport over ​the weekend, while tanker attacks ⁠were reported near the Strait of Hormuz.

The incidents threatened to derail a recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, and have reinforced fears of further ​disruptions along one of the world’s most important energy transit routes.

Ministers of ​OPEC and ⁠non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels of over one-third of the commodity value, impeding efficient movement of crude oil and products.

OPEC has revised down its ⁠oil ​demand growth forecast for this year to 400,000 barrels per ​day from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, in line with developments throughout the year, Haitham Al Ghais, ​Secretary General of the organisation said on Monday.
